components.title: Station access
components.description: Follow the route from the street down to the platform. The building is a teaching composition, not a replica of one station.

components.title: Retaining wall
components.description: This concrete wall holds the soil beside the excavation. It goes in before the station is dug out.

components.title: Temporary braces
components.description: These temporary supports brace the walls during excavation. They disappear as permanent structure takes over.

components.title: Roof and floor slabs
components.description: These permanent levels divide the station and support the structure. In top-down work, the roof is built early.

components.title: Work opening
components.description: Workers and equipment use openings in the roof while digging underneath. The openings close before the finished state.

components.title: Boring machine
components.description: The cutter excavates while material in the chamber supports the face. This is an earth-pressure-balance example.

components.title: Spoil conveyor
components.description: The screw moves spoil out of the chamber; a conveyor carries it rearward. Removal and advance must work together.

components.title: Tunnel rings
components.description: Precast concrete pieces are assembled into the permanent tunnel lining. The segment arrangement here is illustrative.

components.title: Annular grout
components.description: Grout fills the space between the excavation and the outside of the lining. It is separate from the soil-support slurry used for wall construction.

components.title: Monitoring instruments
components.description: Instruments track effects on supports, ground and neighbouring structures. These markers do not show live measurements.

components.title: Freeze pipes and frozen ground
components.description: At Marina Bay, temporary freezing supported one TEL tunnel excavation. This separate historical example does not apply to all MRT tunnels.

components.title: Railway systems
components.description: Track, power, signalling and trains need integration and testing before service, and continued inspection and renewal afterwards.

stops.title: The journey today
stops.body: Start above ground, then follow the station down to the platform. This is a completed teaching section, with construction equipment removed.

stops.title: Why a railway?
stops.body: Rail connects homes and jobs while freeing scarce surface space. Explore the geographic network and the historic decision before returning underground.

stops.title: Find room underground
stops.body: Foundations, utilities and operating rail constrain the work. Investigation informs the method; these layers are schematic, not borehole records.

stops.title: Hold the ground
stops.body: Create a wall panel before excavating the station. Scrub from the supported trench to reinforcement and the completed panel.

stops.title: Build beneath the roof
stops.body: Compare two supported sequences. Top-down builds the roof early; bottom-up builds upward after excavation. Neither is universal.

stops.title: Bore and line
stops.body: Look inside the EPB machine. Control the illustrative advance, inspect spoil removal, then assemble the lining and fill the outside gap.

stops.title: Protect the city
stops.body: Support and monitoring work together. At Rochor, road and canal diversions maintained access and drainage during the works.

stops.title: A temporary frozen barrier
stops.body: Separate case: Marina Bay TEL. Frozen zones around pipes supported a lower tunnel excavation; the upper tunnel used different treatment.

stops.title: From concrete to service
stops.body: A finished civil structure is not yet a railway. Inspect the railway systems, then return to the completed station. Testing and maintenance continue the story.
